A MONUMENT WITH A PLAYFUL SIDE

Explore the fountain.

Look a little closer. There’s a story in the stone,
the steps, and that spectacular arc.

Tap a marker to get to know the details. ↓

DETAIL 01 / 03

The sundial

A sculptural sundial crowns the upper basin. It brings a slower measure of time to a fountain best known for its hourly burst.

The architect’s design notes ↗

DETAIL 02 / 03

The stepped basins

Water spills over two sets of semicircular granite steps. Lohan’s design evokes the continental divide near Chicago, where waterways lead toward different oceans.

The architect’s design notes ↗

DETAIL 03 / 03

The water cannon

The riverfront nozzle throws a high arc across the Chicago River. The architect described that arc as a water-borne echo of the city’s bascule bridges.

The architect’s design notes ↗

TWO KINDS OF WATER THEATER

A cascade to linger by.
A cannon to wait for.

The stepped cascade sends water gently down the granite. The cannon is the timed event: an arc that stretches over the river for five minutes at the top of each scheduled hour.

Two warning lights alert passing river traffic to cannon activity. Our virtual cannon borrows that sequence; its timing and boat challenge are a simulation.

Fountain operation · MWRD ↗

THE ARCHITECT

Dirk Lohan
& Lohan Associates

Lohan Associates completed the fountain in 1989 as part of the Cityfront Center public realm. Dirk Lohan, grandson of Ludwig Mies van der Rohe, brought an architectural eye to a meeting of stone, water, and city.

Chicago Architecture Center ↗

THE NAME

Nicholas J. Melas

Melas served on the water district’s board for 30 years, including 18 as its president. The fountain bears his name and marks the district’s 100th anniversary in 1989.

About the dedication ↗
1989

A CENTURY OF WATER WORK

A birthday for the district.
A tribute to the river.

The district was established in 1889. Its great river reversal came in 1900. The fountain’s centennial honors the institution’s first hundred years, with the reversal at the heart of its story.

Why Chicago reversed its river ↗
